text: Track 4.1 On this week's podcast, I'll be talking about a festival close to my heart, Dongjue, and in particular, the dumpling, a type of traditional Chinese food. I'm from China. That's why this festival is a special event for me. To understand this celebration, first you have to know about the winter solstice, which is when Dongjue takes place. The winter solstice is the shortest day of the year. This means that after it, the days start to get longer and the nights get shorter. The day of the solstice changes every year, but for people in the northern parts of the world, it's usually around the 21st of December. For those of you in the south, it's around June 20th. Dongjue means the extreme of winter, and it shows the light winning over the dark. Personally, I don't really like winter, but for me, Dongjue is one of the best things about it. Due to the nature of our modern world, families don't get the opportunity to spend much time together anymore. They work in different cities or countries. It seems to me that Dongjue is an occasion to bring families together, a time when different generations can interact with one another. And one thing is certain. All families will eat the most famous Chinese comfort food there is. Tainu'en. I love these sweet dumplings, and they remind me of my childhood. Tainu'en are sweet and round, and they are about the size of a table tennis ball. The traditional way of making them is to fill them with sesame seeds or red beans. Then they are boiled, you can fry them too, and served in a sweet soup. This is the way they taste best. Their round shape is to show a coming together, suitable for when a family gets together, right? A little history about these delicious dumplings then. People say Tainu'en are over 1000 years old, and they come from the time of the Tang dynasty. People back then began eating a ball of rice, sesame seeds, fat and sugar. They've had several names over the centuries, but during the 20th century, they became Tainu'en. This means round balls in soup. I think that it's quite a boring name for a food with such long history. During Dongjiu, the dumplings, which are usually white, are coloured, red or pink. The reason for this is that they bring people good luck. For a lot of older Chinese people, Dongjiu is an anniversary. They believe people become a year older on Dongjiu, rather than on their birthdays. People also believe that if you eat too Tainu'en, you will be lucky, and that a married person should leave too in the bowl so their wishes come true. But I'm not convinced. I don't really believe in superstitions, but it doesn't matter. It's nice to see that some traditions aren't dying out.
